# Programming languages, subroutines and compilers (`programming_languages_compilers`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/computing.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Computing, control & information theory (`computing`)
- Deps: needs programmable_computer; helped by symbolic_algebra, algorithm_concept, turing_machine_computability
- Core idea: Writing programs as the numbers a machine obeys is slow and full of errors. Since a program is only data, let the computer translate: the programmer writes in a notation close to algebra and plain words, such as x = (a + b) / 2 or 'repeat for i from 1 to 100', and a translating program (compiler) turns this into machine instructions, assigns the memory cells and reports mistakes. Pieces used often, such as a square root, are written once as subroutines, kept in a library and called by name. With a compatible compiler and the same language facilities, the same source text can run on different makes of machine, and a good compiler produces code almost as fast as that of a skilled hand coder.
- Pitfalls:
  - Assuming that machine time is too precious to spend on translation; this was the main objection in the early 1950s, and programmers' time soon cost more than machines
  - Believing that a language close to English removes the need to think exactly
  - Expecting programs to be right when first written; testing and finding errors take most of the time, as Wilkes noticed in 1949
  - Too many incompatible languages and dialects, which destroys the gain of portability
- History: europe: 1942–1945 – Zuse's Plankalkül (not implemented, published much later); 1949–1951 subroutine library and initial orders for EDSAC (Wheeler, Wilkes, Gill, Cambridge); 1958–1960 ALGOL, a joint European and American design; americas: 1952 – Grace Hopper's A-0 system; 1954–1957 FORTRAN (Backus, IBM); 1958 LISP (McCarthy); 1959–1960 COBOL; 1972 C (Ritchie, Bell Labs)
- Read:
  - Maurice V. Wilkes, David J. Wheeler & Stanley Gill, The Preparation of Programs for an Electronic Digital Computer (1951)
  - Richard L. Wexelblat (ed.), History of Programming Languages (1981)
